newsitem.title: USA: Gore alters claim on charge card calls.
newsitem.headline: Gore alters claim on charge card calls.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore's office on Wednesday was forced to retract his claim that he charged fund-raising calls to the Democratic Party and said the cost was paid by President Clinton's re-election campaign.
During a news conference Monday, Gore said he had used a Democratic National Committee credit card to pay for calls he made from the White House to raise money for party coffers.

"On Monday, the vice president said that a political calling card was used to make phone calls on behalf of the DNC," said Lorraine Voles, the vice president's communications director, in a statement.
"And that was indeed the case. However, the calling card was issued by the Clinton-Gore campaign, not the DNC," Voles said.
Lynn Utrecht, the general counsel for the campaign, said in a telephone interview that the total costs of the charges made by Gore were still being determined.
"We are trying to determine the charges now and expect to be reimbursed" by the DNC, she said. "People make mistakes and that is what happened here."
She said the Clinton-Gore campaign had issued two telephone credit cards to the vice president's office. "We are still trying to determine the costs" that apply to Gore's calls on behalf of the DNC.
Gore said he made telephone calls in December 1995 and the spring of 1996 to donors trying to raise money for the Democratic Party.
He insisted that he had violated no laws by making the solicitations from his White House offices, which an administration source said involved about 50 telephone calls.

Republican congressional leaders have challenged Gore's claim that no laws were violated and have called upon Attorney General Janet Reno to name an independent special counsel to investigate Democratic fund-raising practices.
Sen. Orrin Hatch of Utah said Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee were expected to agree on Thursday to make a formal request to Reno for a counsel.
Reno has said she has not ruled out creating an independent counsel but that she would not do so unless an ongoing Justice Department investigation produces evidence it was necessary.
